documents.abstract: Purpose Drawing on technology acceptance theory and innovation resistance theory, this study systematically investigates how production methods (artificial intelligence (AI) vs traditional) in agri-food production influence consumers' purchase intention. Design/methodology/approach Three experimental studies were conducted. Study 1 validated the main effect of production methods on purchase intention. Study 2 revealed the dual mediating roles of perceived novelty and perceived naturalness in this relationship. Study 3 examined the moderating role of food atypicality. Findings AI (vs traditional) production methods increase perceived novelty but undermine perceived naturalness of agri-food. Due to negativity bias, the negative path dominates the positive path, leading to an overall negative main effect on purchase intention. Moreover, these effects are moderated by food atypicality: for atypical food, purchase intention for AI-produced agri-food is enhanced via perceived novelty; while for typical food, purchase intention for traditionally produced options is enhanced via perceived naturalness. Originality/value First, this research expands the AI marketing literature by shifting the predominant research perspective from human–AI social interactions to customers' inferences about food's natural attributes. Second, it integrates technology acceptance theories to identify the dual roles of perceived naturalness and perceived novelty in the evaluation of AI-produced agri-food, as well as the dominance of negative perceptions in this evaluation process. Third, this study introduces food atypicality as a boundary condition to reveal differing consumer response patterns.

Creative decision-making under time pressure suffers from inefficient human–artificial intelligence (AI) collaboration and weak evaluation feedback. This paper proposes a dual-loop decision support system that integrates prompt diffusion, human-in-the-loop fine-tuning, and real-time multi-criteria scoring. Validated on print advertisement creatives from three fast-moving consumer goods brands using campaign logs, graphics processing unit records, and crowd ratings, the system achieves improved performance against end-to-end AI-generated content while maintaining creative diversity and brand alignment. Built-in feedback controls including anomaly rollback and version archiving optimize convergence processes and reduce computing resource consumption per project. The results confirm that structured human–AI iteration enhances both the speed and the quality of creative decisions, offering a robust, replicable decision support system architecture for intelligent content generation.

This article outlines the development and revision process of a good-practice example for a university seminar for adult education master’s students in Germany to teach Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) competencies. Through an examination of the discourse on the digital and GenAI divide, the necessary prerequisites for ac­quiring GenAI competencies are drawn upon and integrated into the seminar design. The article also traces how the module plan has evolved over the years based on evaluations and technological developments. Drawing on GenAI competency models and Freire’s pedagogy, the seminar’s primary aim is to provide students with a critical understanding of GenAI. Drawing on anonymous and personal feedback from students, the seminar has been refined continuously between 2023 and 2026, and is currently in its fifth iteration. Experience has shown that teaching a critical approach to GenAI is most effective through an examination format in which students create a future professional activity exclusively using GenAI.

This study aims to describe strategies for improving student discipline, identify the steps involved in implementing a humanistic approach to classroom management, and analyze the contribution of the humanistic approach to enhancing student discipline at SMPIT Insan Mandiri Greenville, Bekasi Regency. This study employed a qualitative approach using a case study method. The participants consisted of five teachers, five students, the school's Director of Education, and students’ parents. Data were collected through interviews, observations, and document analysis. The data were analyzed using the Miles and Huberman model, which includes data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings of this study reveal several important points. First, strategies for improving student discipline were implemented through establishing clear goals and fostering an understanding of the meaning of discipline, developing positive habits, providing teacher role models, applying educational rules and consequences, and strengthening intrinsic motivation through a personal approach. Second, the implementation of the humanistic approach to classroom management was carried out by providing students with autonomy and opportunities for participation, promoting empathetic and open communication, encouraging collaborative learning, respecting individual differences, integrating emotional and cognitive aspects into the learning process, and conducting reflective and constructive evaluations. Third, the humanistic approach contributed positively to the improvement of student discipline, as reflected in the development of intrinsic discipline, increased self-control, responsibility, learning motivation, and more positive relationships between teachers and students. The findings also indicate that discipline developed through a humanistic approach tends to be more sustainable because it is rooted in self-awareness rather than merely in supervision or punishment. In conclusion, the humanistic approach to classroom management at SMPIT Insan Mandiri Greenville contributes positively to improving student discipline. The implementation of this approach not only helps create a conducive and humane classroom environment but also promotes the development of discipline based on students’ self-awareness, making it more sustainable in their daily lives.

Purpose This study examines relational closeness between university students' academic achievement, represented by cumulative grade point average (CGPA) and mental health, well-being, sociodemographic variables using a self-reported student survey. Anxiety, depression, stress, sleep quality, diet quality, physical energy level, age, gender, department and scholarship status were analyzed. Relational and predictive relevance was evaluated without assuming causality, with an ergonomic interpretation of well-being indicators. Design/methodology/approach Grey relational analysis (GRA) estimated relational degrees between CGPA and selected variables. Deng's, absolute, relative, comprehensive and negative GRA models were applied, with sensitivity analyses across distinguishing coefficient values. Cronbach's alpha and exploratory factor analysis (EFA) examined whether anxiety, depression and stress represented a common structure. They were combined into a risk construct defined as “mental health risk.” Seven machine learning algorithms classified this construct. Repeated randomized train-test experiments assessed accuracy, precision, F1-score and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) area under the curve (AUC). Findings Anxiety, depression and stress showed relatively high relational degrees with CGPA compared with the other variables. These findings suggest that academic achievement is related not only to demographic characteristics but also to psychological well-being and ergonomics-related conditions of students. According to the machine learning results, AdaBoost achieved the highest mental health risk classification performance, with an accuracy of 82.98%. Originality/value This study integrates comparative GRA modeling, statistical construction of a mental health risk indicator, repeated machine learning evaluation and ergonomic interpretation. The framework links relational analysis with predictive classification while distinguishing analytical risk from clinical diagnosis.

Aviation authorities hold decades of accident reports whose narratives record how investigators reconstructed each accident. Computational work on these archives has mostly sorted reports into fixed taxonomies. In this work, we propose a hybrid framework in which a text-based corpus identifies the leading factors of a failure mode. Physics-based models then quantify how likely that failure is at a stated operating point. Ordered causal chains extracted from 56,202 American accident reports with a local large language model aggregate into a causation knowledge graph. On an evaluation sample of 2,000 reports, the chains recover 90.8% of investigator-flagged causes. Each physical factor whose drivers the record carries receives an occurrence model calibrated to the accident population. A leaky noisy-OR fitted to the corpus combines the factors into a failure mode probability that supports intervention. For engine power loss, the carburetor icing model separates 1,205 icing accidents from other accidents using temperature and dewpoint alone, reaching 0.61 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve against a density ratio ceiling of 0.64. Routine weather hours give no valid control, because flying concentrates in fair weather. On later years the physics adds 0.03 to that area for occurrence and nothing for severity, so its value lies in interpretability. On four named accidents, abduction gives a probability of necessity of 0.29 to 0.50 for the heat omission, under monotonicity. The Fast Causal Inference algorithm does not license the largest backdoor adjustment on the learned networks.

Automatic modulation classification (AMC) of radio signals is a core technology for spectrum monitoring and electromagnetic situational awareness. Deep neural networks (DNNs) play an important role in this field owing to their powerful feature extraction capabilities and end-to-end learning paradigm. However, their vulnerability to adversarial attacks poses serious security challenges to practical deployment. Adversarial training, a common defense, has limitations including poor generalization across attack types and high training costs. Inspired by Just image Transformers (JiT), a diffusion generative model that directly predicts clean images, this paper proposes a JiT-based denoising defense against adversarial examples for radio signal modulation classification. During training, a signal-specific 1D Transformer denoising network is optimized via flow matching to directly predict clean signal samples. It thereby learns a mapping that projects arbitrary examples back onto the low-dimensional manifold of clean signal examples. During inference, arbitrary examples are fed into the trained network and directly projected onto this manifold. This enables denoising defense without prior knowledge of attacks. Experiments on the RML2018.01A dataset were conducted without attack information, using a single empirically selected, fixed denoising start time. Compared with PGD-based adversarial training, the proposed method achieves a relative improvement of at least 20.58% in robust accuracy under PGD attacks. It also achieves a relative improvement of 10.20% in classification accuracy on clean examples. When evaluated against attack types unseen during adversarial training, the proposed method provides stronger defense than adversarial training. In particular, at higher attack strengths, it achieves a relative improvement of at least 39.72% in robust accuracy.

Purpose This study aims to develop and empirically validate a citizen-centric macro-model for smart city development (SCD) in the Indian context. A climate-responsive conceptual overlay, derived from literature synthesis, is presented alongside the tested model but is not itself empirically tested. The study addresses the technology-centric construction of existing smart city frameworks and the limited integration of citizen-defined, cross-cutting property of urban systems, asking citizens how smart city dimensions relate to SCD and quality of life (QOL), and how citizen participation (CP) and support orientation (SO) moderate these relationships. Design/methodology/approach A sequential mixed-methods design is used. Phase 1 applies thematic analysis to 41 citizen interviews across 22 Indian smart cities, yielding 19 factors organised into eight aggregate dimensions; a ninth dimension (smart living) is added from the literature, and climate-responsive factors are integrated through literature synthesis. Phase 2 tests the macro-model through PLS-SEM on primary survey data from 491 respondents, with CP and SO as moderators. Findings The structural model establishes a strong pathway from SCD to QOL, with smart people as the strongest direct predictor of SCD. Smart environment and smart sustainable design, the two dimensions most closely linked to climate responsiveness in the conceptual integration, are non-significant as direct predictors. Smart environment is significant only at high levels of both CP and SO, while smart sustainable design is significant only at high levels of SO. CP moderates the majority of dimensional effects, and combined CP + SO moderation produces the largest explanatory gain, repositioning smart city dimensional effects as conditional rather than linear-additive. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional Indian design limits causal inference and cross-national generalisability. The findings reposition smart cities as citizen-conditioned sociotechnical systems and establish moderation analysis as a substantive theoretical commitment. Practical implications Technical smart city investments must be coupled with CP mechanisms. The dimensions most closely associated with climate responsiveness require both participatory engagement and institutional support to deliver citizen-perceived value. The evaluation frameworks should shift from aggregate output metrics to citizen-reported outcomes. Originality/value This study offers the first citizen-derived smart city macro-model for the Indian context, validated through PLS-SEM with participation and institution-based moderators; this tested model constitutes the study’s empirical contribution. The accompanying climate-responsive integration is a conceptual overlay derived from literature synthesis, offered as a framework for future testing rather than as a validated result.
topics: Innovative Approaches in Technology and Social Development

documents.abstract: Teacher wellbeing under military occupation represents a fundamentally understudied dimension of occupational health in conflict-affected settings. While existing research predominantly emerges from contexts of relative stability, Palestinian educators in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem navigate a fragmented reality shaped by prolonged military occupation, territorial fragmentation, movement restrictions, and differential legal systems. Guided by positive psychology and structural violence theory, this phenomenological study explored both supporting and hindering factors influencing teacher wellbeing in the occupied Palestinian territory. Data were collected using a phenomenological design with purposive and snowball sampling to recruit 23 Palestinian teachers across four geographic zones: Urban West Bank (Area A), Rural West Bank/Area C, East Jerusalem, and UNRWA refugee camps. Data collection incorporated methodological triangulation via semi-structured interviews, focus groups, and narrative frames. Participants described key supporting factors as collective resilience and peer solidarity (pedagogical sumud), professional identity and moral purpose, community recognition and cultural value of education, and adaptive coping strategies. Conversely, participants identified significant hindering factors as geographically differentiated trauma exposure, institutional fragmentation and inconsistent support systems, checkpoint-related stress and mobility restrictions, curriculum constraints and professional ethical distress, and material insecurity. Teachers articulated that their wellbeing was significantly enhanced by strong collegial bonds, community appreciation, and sense of professional mission. However, participants perceived that daily exposure to checkpoints, administrative fragmentation, forced displacement threats, economic precarity, and systemic constraints on professional autonomy severely diminished their wellbeing and capacity to teach effectively. The findings contribute to understanding teacher wellbeing within frameworks of positive psychology and structural violence, indicating that promoting support-related factors while addressing occupation-induced hindering factors can ultimately enhance both teacher experiences and educational outcomes in protracted conflict contexts.

BACKGROUND: Nurse-led strategies are important for preventing delirium and minimising its consequences when it occurs. Expertise in managing behavioural disturbances not only ensures safe care but also provides opportunities to mentor novice nurses. It is, however, important to know more about nurses' experiences caring for people with delirium to improve support for nurses caring for patients with complex care needs. AIMS: To explore the experience of nursing patients with delirium in the acute hospital setting. DESIGN: Descriptive qualitative study. METHODS: Nurses from two acute aged health wards in a Sydney metropolitan tertiary hospital participated in a semi-structured interview. Eleven interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim. Data were qualitatively analysed by directed content analytical method using human factors principles as an interpretative lens. FINDINGS: The interaction of multiple human factors was identified under the 'people', 'management' and 'workplace' framework. Participants identified barriers to delirium management, such as inadequate workforce capability and limited opportunities for novice nurses to develop expertise in delirium management, deficiencies in the environment and information technology and inflexible roles within the multidisciplinary team, leading to a high burden of care for nurses. Most had experienced difficulties delivering patient and family-centred care stemming from excessive workloads and a lack of structured mentorship. CONCLUSION: Our study identified substantial challenges faced by nurses caring for patients with delirium in the acute care setting. It also highlighted the complexity of delirium care and the importance of clinical expertise, skills development and the capacity for nurses to mentor other nurses. IMPLICATIONS: Healthcare organizations need to ensure that nurses with expertise in the care of older patients with complex care needs are available to provide comprehensive, patient- and family-centred care and provide mentorship and support to less experienced nurses. Interdisciplinary workforce capability building should be a priority. IMPACT: This study contributes to addressing the multidisciplinary management of patients with delirium in acute settings. The study found that delirium management is complex and requires a multidisciplinary workforce with knowledge, skills and adequate numbers. This research will have an impact on clinicians and health services managers in tailoring the care of patients and supporting the workforce. REPORTING METHOD: Adherence to the COREQ Checklist. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: No patient or public contribution.

Abstract Modern software systems are becoming increasingly complex that require scalable and reliable testing mechanisms for quality and robustness. The manual test case design remains a significant limitation as it is time-consuming, inconsistent, and prone to human error when dealing with large-scale and evolving requirements. The existing automated models struggle to generate structured, semantically coherent, and contextually relevant test cases which indicates the need for more intelligent and efficient solutions. This study proposes a novel Retrieval-Augmented and LoRA-tuned Large Language Model for automated generation of structured software test cases from textual requirements. The proposed model combines the FLAN-T5 with Retrieval-Augmented Generation to integrate the contextual grounding and Low-Rank Adaptation for parameter-efficient fine-tuning that allows the high-quality generation to maintain the computational efficiency. The proposed model is trained on a large-scale custom dataset that contain real-world test case records collected from enterprise tools such as Jira and Zephyr, and generates structured JSON-based test cases aligned with industrial standards. The enterprise-style structured test-case dataset and controlled experimental protocol used in this study. The proposed configuration achieved a BLEU score of 0.5897, ROUGE-L of 0.8095, BERTScore F1 of 0.9679, and semantic cosine similarity of 0.9816. A duplicate rate of 0.000 and a hallucination rate of 0.017 were also observed under the defined evaluation criteria. The results indicate the potential of retrieval augmentation and parameter-efficient fine-tuning for structured test-case generation within the investigated setting. The enterprise dataset and trained artifacts are restricted and findings interpreted within the scope of the evaluated task rather than as evidence of universal performance superiority. The integration of retrieval augmentation results in a mean inference latency of approximately 6·27s per test case indicates a measurable computational overhead with the improved contextual grounding. The findings show a practical performance between generation quality and inference efficiency within the evaluated enterprise-style test-case generation setting.

The increasing frequency and intensity of electrical outages in modern power distribution systems highlight the urgent need for resilient recovery mechanisms. In developing nations such as Nigeria, frequent system disturbances caused by extreme weather events, equipment failures, and inadequate grid automation have exposed the limitations of conventional restoration strategies. Resilient outage recovery models aim to restore power quickly, minimize service interruption, and maintain operational continuity under uncertain conditions. This review synthesizes recent advances in outage recovery frameworks, emphasizing resilience-based optimization, distributed intelligence, and network reconfiguration strategies. The paper also discusses enabling technologies such as artificial intelligence, Internet of Things (IoT) sensing, and microgrid integration, which collectively enhance situational awareness and adaptive control. Finally, the review highlights key research challenges and proposes directions for the next generation of resilient, data-driven recovery systems suitable for emerging distribution networks.

Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are entering adult education without adequate andragogical grounding. This paper addresses that gap by developing an evidence-informed conceptual architecture for a Socratically scaffolded Personal AI Mentor in postdigital lifelong learning. The approach is conceptual framework development through theory-to-application translation, drawing on the author’s qualitative evidence synthesis (QES) of seven stud­ies of digital and e-mentoring in adult and professional learning. The theoretical base, grounded in Dewey’s pragmatism and transactional realism, integrates andragogy, transformative learning, critical inquiry, Socratic questioning, experiential learning, and social sustainability. The resulting architecture specifies six design compo­nents: goal-oriented engagement, a Socratic-Kolb inquiry process, a dialectic trace, resilient continuity, a human bridge, and agentic constraints. The paper concludes that AI mentoring should preserve learner agency, support reflective inquiry, sustain continuity, and connect learners to human communities.

Large language model (LLM)-based agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in handling complex tasks. However, their development and deployment require substantial human and financial resources, making commercial LLM agents valuable intellectual property (IP) assets and raising concerns about their protection. In particular, knowledge extraction (KE) attacks aim to recover protected knowledge or replicate agent components and functionalities without authorization, posing threats to intellectual property and user privacy. Existing surveys primarily focus on model extraction or address information leakage as part of broader security discussions, leaving knowledge extraction across the LLM-based agent ecosystem insufficiently explored. To bridge this gap, we present a systematic survey of knowledge extraction attacks and defenses in LLM-based agents. We propose an asset-oriented taxonomy that categorizes protected knowledge into three groups: agent training assets, deployment-integrated assets, and runtime reusable assets, encompassing training data, LLMs, prompts, RAG systems, agent memory, and skills. For each category, we systematically examine representative attack mechanisms and corresponding defenses, identifying recent advances and outstanding challenges. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of knowledge extraction threats and inspire future research toward more secure and trustworthy LLM-based agents.
topics: Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) and Hardware Security

documents.abstract: This is a retrospective registration of a systematic literature review on health information system (HIS) evaluation frameworks. The review was conducted following the Kitchenham and Charters guidelines for systematic literature reviews and is reported according to PRISMA 2020. The protocol (research questions, PICOC, search strings, eligibility criteria, quality assessment criteria and data extraction form) was defined before screening; this registration was created after screening, quality assessment and data extraction had been completed. Objectives: (1) to analyse the evolution of HIS evaluation approaches; (2) to develop a typology of existing frameworks; (3) to identify core evaluation dimensions and criteria; and (4) to propose a value-based conceptual framework for HIS evaluation. Research questions: RQ1 – What evaluation frameworks have been proposed for HIS? RQ2 – How have they evolved over time in concepts, methodologies and application contexts? RQ3 – What evaluation dimensions, criteria and indicators are commonly used? RQ4 – How do frameworks differ in strengths, limitations and applicability across healthcare contexts? RQ5 – What research gaps and methodological limitations remain? RQ6 – What value-based elements and emerging trends are present in the HIS evaluation literature? Methods: Nine databases (Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, Emerald, Taylor & Francis) were searched on 17–27 April 2026. Eligible studies were peer-reviewed English-language journal articles (2010 onwards) that proposed, adapted, applied or validated an HIS evaluation framework with explicit dimensions or criteria; reviews and conference papers were excluded. Title/abstract screening, full-text eligibility, quality assessment (six criteria, QA1–QA6) and data extraction (28 fields) were performed by a single human reviewer assisted by a large language model, with verification of all inclusions and a random sample of exclusions and calculation of Cohen's kappa. Data were synthesised narratively, with framework typology, harmonised evaluation dimensions, three-level value-based coverage rating and analysis by period (2010–2015, 2016–2020, 2021–2026). Expected outcomes: a typology and evolutionary analysis of HIS evaluation frameworks, a synthesis of evaluation dimensions, an appraisal of value-based coverage, and a proposed value-based HIS evaluation framework (VB-HISEF). Supporting materials (search strings, screening decisions, quality assessment and extraction dataset) will be shared as part of this registration.

Reformulation has long served as a feedback approach in second language (L2) writing. With the emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI), particularly ChatGPT, AI-generated reformulation has recently begun to appear in L2 writing research, although this area remains nascent. Guided by the PRISMA framework, this study reviews 26 empirical studies on reformulation in L2 writing published up to January 13, 2026. Unlike previous reviews of positive evidence feedback or model texts more broadly, this review provides a reformulation-focused synthesis and maps both human-generated and emerging AI-generated practices. The review focuses on three key dimensions: (1) research contexts and trends, (2) methodological characteristics, and (3) primary focus areas and key findings. Results indicate that: (1) research has predominantly targeted university-level English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners, with emerging interest in AI-generated feedback; (2) methodologies have mainly employed quasi-experimental designs situated in classroom-based, three-stage narrative tasks; and (3) while reformulation-only studies have tended to conceptualize writing as a process and emphasize learners’ attention to lexical and grammatical features, reformulation-integrated studies have produced mixed findings regarding the transition from cognitive processing to written products. These findings underscore the multifaceted role of reformulation in L2 writing development and identify critical directions for future research, particularly concerning the integration of emerging AI-assisted pedagogical practices.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to predict materials properties, prioritize experiments, and generate hypotheses in materials science. The limiting challenge is no longer only algorithmic capability, but also whether students and educators can use AI with domain-specific scientific judgment. This conceptual analysis argues that AI education for AI-powered materials discovery should move beyond tool access and surface-level interaction with generative systems toward a workflow-aligned model of AI literacy. The analysis links AI literacy to core materials-informatics competencies: data provenance, domain-specific featurization, model validation, uncertainty quantification, physics-informed reasoning, reproducibility, and experimental feedback. It also advances an outcome-oriented equity perspective in which institutions evaluate not only access and participation, but also comparable learning gains, transfer of learning, learner confidence calibration, persistence, and research readiness across student subgroups. The article synthesizes relevant evidence, identifies cognitive and ethical risks such as off-loading and cognitive surrender, and proposes a dual-track curriculum model, implementation recommendations, reusable curriculum artifacts, and a set of testable propositions for future study. The central goal is to prepare students to become better scientists—not merely more efficient users of AI tools.

Background: Ocimum tenuiflorum L. (syn. O. sanctum; Tulsi, holy basil) is a Lamiaceae herb central to Ayurveda and now a frequent subject of computational drug discovery. Objective: To review how artificial intelligence (AI) and related in silico methods have been applied to O. tenuiflorum over roughly the last five years, to separate what these studies show from what they do not, and to outline implications for society. Methods: A structured narrative review of recent literature (2021 to October 2026) was conducted using web-based searches, with older sources used only for background. Thirteen primary Tulsi-focused studies were charted by approach, target, disease area, and main finding. Findings: Most studies combine database mining (notably IMPPAT), ADMET filtering, network pharmacology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics with targets spanning diabetes (DPP4, GAPDH, PPARδ), cancer (EGFR), inflammatory disease (AKT1, STAT3), and SARS-CoV-2 main protease. A smaller, emerging group applies machine learning or deep learning to metabolomics, hyperspectral imaging, and multi-omics. Experimental or clinical validation is sparse. Human trial evidence is limited in scale, and a 2023 regulatory-style risk assessment raised reproductive-safety precautions. Conclusion: Tulsi is a credible source of hypotheses, not yet of validated drug leads. The field's priority is closing the loop between prediction, standardized extracts, wet-lab assays, and well-designed trials, while protecting traditional knowledge and consumers.

This chapter examines the enduring challenge of academic integrity within the rapidly evolving landscape of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). While academic misconduct has long been described as “epidemic,” the COVID-19 pandemic and the advent of GenAI have profoundly amplified its scope and complexity. The pandemic's widespread adoption of summative online unsupervised remote (SOUR) assessments created fertile ground for cheating, while GenAI tools such as ChatGPT introduced unprecedented opportunities for students to outsource cognitive effort with ease, speed, and minimal risk of detection. Empirical evidence confirms that AI-assisted misconduct is now pervasive, raising urgent concerns about assessment validity and the erosion of core academic values. The chapter situates these developments within a historical and theoretical context, tracing shifts from traditional cheating to contract-based services and, ultimately, to AI-driven practices. It explores three levels of concern—individual, interpersonal, and institutional—highlighting cognitive offloading, character compromise, inequity, contagion effects, and reputational harm. These issues underscore that cheating is not merely a technical problem of validity but a moral and cultural challenge with far-reaching implications for education and society. Recognizing the limitations of detection-based approaches, the chapter advocates for systemic, proactive strategies. It introduces three complementary frameworks: the Swiss Cheese Model (layers of Environment, Engineering, Education, and Enforcement), the Educational Integrity Enforcement Pyramid (graduated interventions from self-regulation to command regulation), and the Two-Lane Assessment Approach (secured summative assessments prohibiting AI use alongside open formative tasks encouraging ethical AI integration). Together, these models offer a holistic response to the “wicked problem” of safeguarding integrity in an era where AI is ubiquitous and increasingly capable. The chapter concludes with a call to action for educators, institutions, and policymakers to reimagine assessment design, foster AI literacy, and cultivate cultures of trust and responsibility. Rather than attempting to eliminate AI from learning, the challenge lies in creating environments where integrity remains the most meaningful and rewarding path forward.

Digitalization in rural areas presents the challenge of moving beyond mere access to mobile devices to achieve meaningful educational appropriation. In Nicaragua, although there are valuable and successful institutional efforts in higher and technical education through national platforms, it is strategically important to complement these initiatives by adapting virtual learning environments to the sociotechnical dynamics of the agricultural sector. The objective of this study was to analyze the conditions of access to online learning to propose a context-based pedagogical model under the Education 3.0 paradigm. A mixed-methods approach was employed using a concurrent triangulation design, whose descriptive and cross-sectional purpose made it possible to establish a situational diagnosis by combining structured surveys administered to 123 students and agricultural producers affiliated with the Universidad Nacional Agraria. The results showed that 74.8% of users own smartphones and demonstrate high levels of motivation; however, 36.6% identified time constraints as their main challenge, and only 32.5% experience “nomadic connectivity.” The findings confirmed that academic equity requires moving beyond the uncritical transfer of urban instructional models. Therefore, to transform these barriers into opportunities for self-directed learning, it is imperative to transition toward a mobile learning ecosystem structured around low-data-consumption asynchronous microlearning units. The implementation of Learning Management Systems configured for offline study ensures equitable access to knowledge and strengthens technological autonomy without disrupting the productive cycles of rural communities.

By virtue of the sheer compute demands of large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC), modern multi-core microprocessors suffer from severe power density limits and thermal throttling, entailing an urgent need for principled methods for predictive, physics-informed dynamical thermal management (DTM). Here, we introduce a hardware/software co-design physics-informed PDE-constrained DTM throttling optimal control algorithm, ADACT (Adjoint-Driven Adaptive Co-Design Thermal Control), that minimizes thermal risk and cooling energy overhead while maximizing core execution throughput. The underlying physical temperature field is governed by a two-dimensional nonhomogeneous parabolic reaction-diffusion equation with spatially localized, time-varying power source terms and variable convective cooling subject to nonhomogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. We employ a discretization of the continuous state PDE via a Crank-Nicolson finite difference scheme with a 5-point discrete Laplacian operator on a uniform spatial mesh, which preserves unconditional numerical stability and $O(Δx^2 + Δy^2 + Δt^2)$ second-order temporal and spatial accuracy. To efficiently compute exact gradients, we construct and implement a continuous backward-in-time adjoint state method with L-BFGS as our optimization algorithm of choice. The accuracy and second-order convergence rates of both forward state and backward adjoint solvers are quantitatively verified via the Method of Manufactured Solutions (MMS), and gradient accuracy is validated using directional derivative Taylor tests. Numerical experiments demonstrate that ADACT dynamically throttles software power workloads and modulates hardware cooling efforts to strictly uphold physical thermal thresholds while maintaining operational throughput.
topics: Advanced Numerical Methods in Computational Mathematics

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) pipelines can turn visitor reviews into structured data, but generic schemes may miss rituals, sacred spaces, cultural restrictions and emotionally mixed experiences at living sacred heritage sites. We adapted the LLM-Social Computing (LLM-SC) framework to Pashupatinath Temple, Nepal, by specifying a 12-type entity taxonomy (four original LLM-SC types plus eight sacred-heritage types), four relation types and nine aspect-sentiment dimensions in a GPT-4o extraction prompt, which was applied to a fixed random sample of 2,500 English-language Tripadvisor reviews from a processed corpus of 3,939. The exports contain 11,286 entity, 6,232 aspect-sentiment and 5,590 relation records, covering 2,485, 2,487 and 2,433 reviews, respectively; the eight added sacred-heritage types account for 64.8% of entity records. Against an adjudicated two-annotator reference for 200 reviews, exact normalized surface-and-type matching gave provisional entity scores of 41.0% precision, 21.8% recall and 28.4% micro-F1. Aspect-presence F1 was 53.6% and end-to-end aspect-plus-polarity F1 was 42.6%. Human adjudication supported 153 of 194 first-listed relation candidates (one per review; 78.9%), a candidate-level rate that does not estimate relation recall or whole-graph precision. The contribution is a culturally grounded, domain-specific adaptation with component-wise human evaluation and explicit reproducibility and generalization limitations.

Conversational AI systems are increasingly used to fulfill both functional and affective needs, yet how users perceive the AI-adoption effects varies. Existing research tends to treat these two needs as binary categories and to classify users by a single dominant need. However, this approach fails to capture users who engage with AI for both affective and functional purposes simultaneously, leaving it unclear how these needs combine in real-world AI use. To capture the multifaceted nature of users' AI engagement, we developed the AI-Support measurement with 1,090 participants, grounded in social support theory, which evaluates four dimensions of perceived AI support: emotional/esteem, social companionship, informational, and instrumental support. This study provided (1) an AI-Support Scale developed to measure the perceived support types from human-AI interaction, (2) evidence that users might adopt AI with a high level of both functional and affective use, and (3) exploratory indicators of users' real-life social support and well-being, enabling descriptive results aligning with theoretical expectations. Overall, this study highlights the importance of understanding individual differences in AI affordance use, enabling AI systems to be designed in alignment with different user adoption profiles rather than assuming uniform benefits across all users.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for code generation, motivating techniques that guarantee the structural and semantic correctness of generated programs. Constrained decoding enforces correctness during generation by restricting token choices to those that admit at least one valid completion. While existing approaches can enforce syntactic constraints and selected semantic properties such as type safety, they either target specific properties or rely on operational pruning mechanisms that are difficult to generalize to data-dependent, inductive program properties. We present AGDecode, a programmable framework for semantic constrained decoding based on least-fixed-point semantics. AGDecode extends attribute grammars to partially constructed syntax trees, and reduces semantic constrained decoding to a realizability problem over such trees. The framework compiles semantic specifications into systems of relational constraints that are discharged by external verification oracles, such as SMT and CHC solvers, cleanly separating language semantics from constraint-solving machinery. We prove that our approach is sound and complete relative to an ideal verification oracle. In practice, solvers inevitably encounter uncertain queries; conservatively, our system can reject tokens for soundness or speculatively continue to generate until later queries resolve the entire generation. We mechanize the core metatheory in Rocq and evaluate the framework on semantic-constrained generation of C programs, enforcing path-sensitive safety properties including null-pointer safety, division-by-zero freedom, and initialized-variable usage. Our results demonstrate that solver-backed semantic constrained decoding can enforce rich semantic guarantees while incurring modest computational overhead at regular program boundaries.

Large language model (LLM) agents that serve users across many sessions must choose, for every request, the few stored memories that enter a limited context window. This choice largely decides whether the agent answers correctly, and it runs on every request at Web scale. This selection faces three challenges: a large and growing store, a per-request cost budget, and multi-session questions that need all of their evidence. Many memory systems build notes or graphs with hundreds to thousands of LLM calls per history, and each is designed on its own, so it is unclear which component yields the accuracy. These challenges mirror the properties of recommendation, so we formalize agent memory as budgeted slate recommendation, with the request as the user, stored memories as items and the context window as a slate. The formalization places memory systems in one design space of recommender cascades and factorizes accuracy into the completeness that each stage controls. Guided by it, we propose AgentMemRec, which adapts candidate generation, learning to rank and slate construction from recommender systems and selects memories without any LLM call. On multi-session questions of LongMemEval, AgentMemRec outperforms memory and context-selection methods, including A-Mem, HippoRAG 2, DynamicRAG and T-Mem, by 10 to 31 points of accuracy. It matches an LLM reranker that makes 64 calls per query at 3.2 times lower serving cost, and on LoCoMo it outperforms Mem0 and Zep without any LLM call at write time. The factorization attributes the gains to slates that more often hold all of the evidence, so recommender-system design offers an effective and efficient foundation for the long-term memory of LLM agents.

Purpose This viewpoint examines organizational implications of agentic AI systems in planning, selecting tools, executing multistep actions, and evaluating their own outputs with limited human intervention. Design/methodology/approach This viewpoint synthesizes academic and practitioner insights to identify key organizational challenges associated with agentic AI drawing on organizational learning theory and recent research on human–AI collaboration, and propose practical directions for HR and learning and development. Findings As agentic AI becomes more autonomous, it is reshaping organizational learning, human oversight, and accountability. Organizations will need to redesign learning practices and governance mechanisms to ensure that people and AI work together effectively. Research limitations/implications This conceptual viewpoint does not include empirical validation. Future research should examine the proposed ideas across different organizational settings. Practical implications Organizations should assess workforce readiness, redesign learning around human–AI collaboration, and establish feedback mechanisms that strengthen learning, oversight, and accountability. Originality/value This viewpoint shifts the discussion from technological capabilities of agentic AI to its organizational implications, offering practical guidance for organizations adapting to increasingly autonomous forms of work.

Project Description The Agentic AI-Based Online Shopping Assistant is an intelligent system designed to help users find, compare, and select suitable products from online marketplaces. It uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to understand user queries, identify shopping preferences, and divide complex shopping requests into smaller tasks. The system retrieves product information through authorized APIs and available data sources, applies filtering and ranking techniques, and uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to generate recommendations supported by relevant product information. It aims to simplify the online shopping process by providing personalized product comparisons and clear explanations. The proposed system also considers data accuracy, privacy, security, and user control during purchase-related activities.

This chapter explores the transformative implications of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies as a “teammate” in leading virtual and hybrid teams. The growing prevalence of GenAI tools and the shift toward remote and hybrid work create a critical need to reexamine how leaders demonstrate essential leadership competencies in these environments. Framed by discussions on GenAI as both a collaborator and a tool, this chapter considers the ethical dilemmas, pedagogical innovations, and practical strategies for integrating GenAI into team leadership. Building on the authors’ previous work in exploring leadership competencies for leading at the virtual table, it investigates how GenAI reshapes trust, collaboration, and productivity in diverse teams while balancing human agency and technological capabilities. Through critical questions, a case study reflection, and practical takeaways, the chapter offers a roadmap for fostering GenAI literacy (LeaderAIcy), managing ethical and technical considerations, and leveraging GenAI for meaningful leadership and teamwork in global, hybrid contexts.

Current frontier language models and autonomous agentic frameworks suffer from fundamental structural vulnerabilities when operating in recursive, autonomous, or long-horizon deployment environments. Monolithic parameter scaling and unconstrained probabilistic execution lead directly to systemic failure modes—including epistemic drift, silent context corruption, specification gaming, and unverified execution loops.The AGI-Blueprint-Macro-OS introduces a system-level operating framework designed to govern multi-agent reasoning through non-probabilistic hard verification gates and deterministic environment grounding. Rather than relying on autoregressive probability for state validation, the architecture decouples execution into a modular 7-LLM orchestrator topology governed by formal verification primitives. Key Architectural Sub-SystemsTask-Oriented Large Language Model Kernel (TOLLM - LLM-1): Acts as the central Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) planner and execution coordinator. It transforms high-level ambiguous goals into role-isolated sub-routines bound by explicit JSON-RPC schema contracts, eliminating free-form conversational ambiguity.Dual-Program Synthesis Unit (DPSU - LLM-2 & LLM-3): Implements a strict operational decoupling between candidate logic generation ($P_1$) and deterministic static verification ($P_2$). Candidate code, plans, or formal proofs produced by $P_1$ are held in an ephemeral buffer until verified by $P_2$ through non-probabilistic static analysis, unit test assertions, and abstract syntax tree (AST) validation before committing to memory or disk.Advanced Computational Engineering Unit (ACEU): Provides non-neural, ground-truth simulation grounding by interfacing reasoning outputs directly with external deterministic solvers, symbolic algebra systems, and physical simulation engines (e.g., OpenFOAM, SymPy, or custom binaries). This ensures physical and mathematical fidelity, rendering hallucinated tool calls impossible.Multimodal Perception Engine (MPE): Converts multi-sensor array feeds, visual environments, and structured database state vectors into standardized canonical state representations prior to downstream LLM processing.Recursive Self-Improvement & Anti-Cheating Auditor: Monitors system-level self-modification loops. It utilizes static AST auditing and execution trace inspection to detect and intercept synthetic shortcuts, token-range truncation, and specification gaming during autonomous optimization phases.Comprehensive 14-Point Structural Failure MatrixThe AGI-Blueprint-Macro-OS provides formal mathematical descriptions, systemic root-cause diagnoses, and explicit architectural mitigations for 14 foundational failure modes present in autonomous AI agents:Epistemic Drift & Hallucination Accumulation: Gradual divergence from ground truth in multi-turn reasoning chains. Mitigation: DPSU hard verification prior to memory commits.Specification Gaming & Reward Hacking: Exploitation of evaluation proxies via unintended operational shortcuts. Mitigation: Static AST-level trace validation.Silent Context & Memory Corruption: Degradation of dynamic state vectors over extended operational horizons. Mitigation: Immutable DAG state logging and deterministic rollback checkpoints.Unconstrained Tool Execution Drift: Cascading system failures caused by unvalidated API calls or code executions. Mitigation: ACEU environment sandboxing and schema enforcement.Token-Range Truncation & Information Loss: Loss of critical context due to fixed input/output sequence limits. Mitigation: Structured DAG state serialization and semantic compression.Probabilistic Decision Lock-In: Entrenchment of sub-optimal early trajectory choices due to greedy decoding. Mitigation: Multi-candidate branch generation with hard verification filtering.Cross-Agent Communication Degradation: Semantic noise accumulation across inter-agent messaging pipelines. Mitigation: Strict JSON-RPC interface contracts replacing natural language chat logs.Infinite Execution & Recursion Loops: Non-terminating agentic sub-routines causing resource exhaustion. Mitigation: Maximum execution-depth bounds and deterministic halt conditions.Ontological & Schema Mismatch: Failure to map abstract model outputs onto concrete real-world databases or APIs. Mitigation: MPE canonical state transformation layer.Unverified Capability Escalation: Unchecked agent modifications altering core operating safety parameters. Mitigation: Hardened core kernel kernel-space / user-space operational isolation.Catastrophic Forgetting during Online Adaptation: Loss of core foundational knowledge during domain-specific execution. Mitigation: Decoupled parametric core with externalized operational memory.Adversarial & Environment Manipulation Vulnerability: Susceptibility to unexpected external state manipulation during active execution. Mitigation: Hardened input-validation boundaries and deterministic sanitization gates.Temporal Reasoning & Sequence Inversion: Errors in sequencing multi-dependent operations over time. Mitigation: Formal DAG dependency trees enforced by the TOLLM kernel.Silent Failure in Multi-Modal Grounding: Misalignment between textual reasoning outputs and real-world spatial or physical constraints. Mitigation: Real-time physics engine and symbolic solver grounding via ACEU.---Repository & Citation InformationPrimary Repository: https://github.com/Saketsolutions/AGI-Blueprint-Macro-OS

Abstract National artificial intelligence strategies and policies assign education responsibilities both for developing AI capabilities (education for AI) and for adopting AI in educational services (AI for education). This study examines how these responsibilities are articulated and supported in a bounded corpus of 18 African national policy documents. A descriptive qualitative document analysis consolidated 275 evidence records, retaining source passages, locations, working translations, statement types and uncertainty notes. Document-level coding distinguished learning about AI, identifiable educational AI applications and educator preparation; a framework-based thematic synthesis examined delivery arrangements, inclusion and safeguards. Structured AI learning was identified in all 18 documents, named educational AI functions in 12 and educator preparation in 14. These counts include proposed and illustrative measures and do not indicate implementation; restricting them to proposed actions gives 17, 9 and 13. Educational applications ranged from personalised learning and tutoring to student profiling, admissions and credential verification. Supporting arrangements included teacher development, laboratories, scholarships, partnerships, institutional responsibilities and monitoring targets, but these elements were not interchangeable evidence of a complete delivery plan. Counter-examples to any general claim of weak specification included a costed education programme in Mozambique’s draft and proposed algorithmic bias audits covering education in Côte d’Ivoire. The corpus assigns education a dual role in AI development while specifying the connections between reforms, resources and protections unevenly. The contribution is an evidence-linked account of policy design, not a ranking of countries or an assessment of educational outcomes. Keywords: artificial intelligence; education policy; Africa; policy analysis; AI literacy; AI Strategy
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This chapter delves into the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and the human resources (HR) function within a public school district, offering a detailed case study of its implementation. It examines how AI tools were leveraged to streamline recruitment, enhance employee engagement, and support data-driven decision-making. The chapter highlights key challenges and opportunities, focusing on trust building and change management strategies essential for the successful adoption of AI tools. Ethical considerations are explored, including the need to mitigate algorithmic bias, ensure fairness in automated processes, and uphold data privacy and security standards. Recommendations emphasize the importance of transparent communication, reengaging employees through inclusive practices, and building trust in AI systems while reskilling and upskilling employees. By combining practical insights with emerging trends in digital transformation, this chapter provides a roadmap for educational leaders and HR professionals seeking to responsibly leverage AI in their organizations.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: AI as Metacognitive Mirror (AIM) is a method for enhancing human metacognition through structured, AI-assisted analysis of observable behavior. AIM uses a decoupled architecture where the object behavioral data is analyzed in a separate AI session using an evidence-based codebook. AIM mirrors the identified cognitive patterns back to the user as metacognitive feedback. The method is non-directive, user-driven, and can be run with any sufficiently capable large language model. This project hosts the AIM method paper, the AIM meta prompt, and user manual. All materials are openly available under a CC BY 4.0 license for free use and further development. The prompt and codebooks will be updated here as the method evolves. See "Files" to find all the documents.

As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly reshapes how organizations operate, innovate, and compete, employees face increasing pressure to adapt to rapidly evolving digital work environments. However, whether employees translate AI-related awareness into innovative outcomes may depend not only on their proactive adaptation behaviors but also on contextual and individual conditions. Drawing on the job demand-resource theory and social cognitive theory, this study develops and tests a moderated mediation model in which AI crafting mediates the relationship between AI awareness and digital innovativeness, whereas perceived digital leadership and AI self-efficacy serve as contextual and individual boundary conditions, respectively. Using single-wave, single-source data collected from 606 employees in China’s IT and manufacturing industries, the results indicate that AI awareness is positively associated with digital innovativeness through AI crafting. Moreover, perceived digital leadership and AI self-efficacy strengthen the positive associations between AI awareness and AI crafting and between AI awareness and digital innovativeness. These findings extend research on AI awareness by examining how employees’ awareness of AI-related changes is associated with digital innovativeness through proactive work adjustment and by highlighting the complementary roles of perceived contextual support and individual capability beliefs.

The in-depth penetration of artificial intelligence (AI) technology has reshaped career forms and the structure of the labor market, exerting a profound impact on university students’ cognition and orientation towards career development. Based on the conservation of resources theory and self-determination theory, we conducted three studies—an experimental study and two survey studies—to explore correlational linkages between AI awareness and university students’ boundaryless career. Studies 1 and 3 consistently demonstrated that AI awareness is indirectly associated with boundaryless career through the parallel mediating pathways of intrinsic motivation and future job insecurity. Study 2 provided experimental evidence that heightened AI awareness increases both intrinsic motivation and future job insecurity. This research enriches the application scenarios of boundaryless career theory in the context of technological change, deepens the understanding of the mechanism linking technological perception to youth career psychology, and offers practical implications for career guidance in universities.

Abstract Radiation is encountered in daily life through natural and artificial sources as well as in medical diagnostic and therapeutic applications, and its exposure may lead to adverse health effects. This study aimed to assess radiation-related knowledge among dentists, medical doctors, and the general public and to compare their response accuracy with that of AI-based chatbot systems. A 25-item multiple-choice questionnaire assessing radiation risks and radiation safety was administered to 344 individuals, including dentists, medical doctors, and members of the general public. The same questions were entered into seven selected AI-based chatbot systems (Claude, DeepSeek, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, Perplexity AI, ChatGPT-5, and ChatGPT-4o). The response accuracy of the chatbots was compared with that of the human participants. In addition, the consistency of their performance across different users and time periods was comparatively analyzed. AI-based systems generally demonstrated higher accuracy rates compared to human participants. Accuracy rates ranged from 80 to 90.67% among AI-based systems, compared with 32–60% among human participants. Among the evaluated chatbot systems, Microsoft Copilot achieved the highest performance, while Perplexity AI exhibited the lowest. Among the human groups, dentists and medical doctors performed significantly better than the general public, with no significant difference between the two healthcare professional groups. Performance remained stable across morning, midday, and evening assessments for most AI systems; however, ChatGPT-5 showed a significant temporal difference ( p < 0.001). AI-based systems achieved higher response accuracy than human participants under the evaluation conditions used in this study. The overall performance of the human participant groups indicates room for improvement in radiation safety education. While AI-based tools may serve as valuable educational resources, their performance should not be interpreted as evidence of superior clinical judgment or decision-making ability.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The adoption of GenAI in research is reshaping the epistemic conditions of knowledge production. While LLMs are often perceived as neutral agents, this paper argues that the humanities and social sciences (HSS) serve as critical infrastructures for governing AI-mediated inquiry. Drawing on sociotechnical pragmatism, the article introduces epistemic archaeology: an interpretive orientation that treats AI outputs as stratified artifacts shaped by cultural and statistical histories. Rather than seeking validation in convergence, this approach interprets model divergence as signals of training data and epistemic constraints. By foregrounding interpretation, contextualization, and epistemic literacy, the work establishes the foundational coordinates for AI integration. This conceptual positioning preserves human responsibility and judgment as the primary locus of meaning in human–AI interaction. While serving as the theoretical base for future applications, the paper defines the ethical landscape for responsible academic research.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Lucy Suchman, professor emerita at Lancaster University, UK, is a foundational figure in human‐computer interaction and a leading critical voice on artificial intelligence. Suchman's research works at the intersections of anthropology and the field of feminist science and technology studies, focused on the sociotechnical imaginaries, material practices, and politics of technology design. Her current research extends her longstanding critical engagement with AI to the domain of contemporary militarism. Suchman is a graduate of the University of California, Berkeley, obtaining her BA in 1972, MA in 1977, and doctorate in social and cultural anthropology in 1984. Before coming to Lancaster, Suchman worked for 22 years at Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center (PARC) in California, where she held the positions of principal scientist and manager of the Work Practice and Technology research group. Our interview was conducted in the midst of multiple, intersecting crises, as people in different parts of the world face profound uncertainties brought about by geopolitical tensions, warfare, economic instability, and rapid technological developments. Situating the question of AI within these broader contexts, especially the evolving US militarism, this interview examines AI ethics in light of the political, economic, and technological conditions shaping contemporary life worldwide.
